prize_parts.citation: for the magic-wavelength optical lattice clock, from Katori's concept to its realisation at the 10^-18 level of systematic uncertainty, which turned a precision instrument into a probe of fundamental physics

statement.case_for: I keep B019 with Katori and Ye as my one-part configuration, and I have not changed it since round 1. The chair asks what is discovered beyond better numbers. My answer is that choosing the magic wavelength makes the trap light shift cancel, so thousands of atoms can be held tightly and interrogated with long coherence and no motional penalty. That is a new physical regime for an atomic reference, not a refinement of the comb or of single-ion control. Once the systematic budget fell to the 10^-18 level, the clock stopped being a metrology exercise: it resolves the gravitational redshift over millimetres, shows many-body collisional and lattice effects in the systematics, and bounds variations of constants. As a theorist who works with experimental groups, I find this the cleanest case on the list of an idea made visible and controllable in a real device. It is also the most mature case. Independent groups at JILA, RIKEN, SYRTE, PTB and NIST have confirmed the budgets, partly through direct clock comparisons. I agree with Kroll that the planned redefinition of the second belongs in neither the citation nor the rationale. I also take Lindroth's point that the citation should name the magic-wavelength concept, so that it does not read as a prize for accuracy records.
statement.case_against: The honest weakness is the line of earlier prizes (laser cooling in 1997 and 2018, the comb in 2005, single-particle control in 2012), and it can be answered only by the physical argument above, not by the maturity record. If the majority sees the lattice clock as a threshold crossed in a long programme and not a single discovery, B047 is the strongest alternative on scientific novelty. The credit also carries open questions. The priority record for the first Sr lattice-clock measurements (Tokyo, JILA, SYRTE) should be checked in the supporting record. Lemonde and Derevianko are outside the names, and I accept Kroll's view that the decisive steps are the concept and the experimental demonstration, but I cannot verify the early record myself from the supplied material.

responses.point: Eriksson asks whether the lattice clock is a single decisive discovery or an instrument that crossed a threshold, and defers to the atomic physicists on whether 10^-18 is a physical discovery or a technical achievement.
responses.response: I will answer as a user of precision quantum devices. Reaching 10^-18 is not a technical milestone, because it required a new physical element: a trap in which the light shift is engineered to vanish for the clock transition, together with control of many-body and collisional shifts in a degenerate Fermi gas. Neither of those is in the comb or ion-trap prizes. I accept that this is a threshold and that the committee may read it as one, and I do not claim it is as clean a new class of matter as your quantum spin Hall effect. That is why B012 is now my second alternative. My doubts there are what they were: the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang proposal sits outside the names, and I still cannot judge how far the 2016 prize covers Z2 topology. Your argument that the 2016 citation concerned a field-driven Chern invariant is a good one, and it has shifted me from doubting the distinctness to doubting only the credit gap. I would still choose maturity plus an unambiguous two-name credit this year.

responses.point: Mehlig argues that B047 is a new regime of matter while the lattice clock is an instrument achievement on top of the comb, and that the prize does not need a settled pairing mechanism.
responses.response: I am more persuaded than in round 1 that the pairing mechanism need not be settled. Your fractional Chern insulator argument is a good test of stability, and the qualitative phase diagram has indeed been seen by many groups. We still differ on weight. Twist-angle disorder and sample-to-sample variation limit what can be claimed quantitatively, and the experimental credit (Cao, Fatemi and the 2018 authors) cannot be repaired within three names. In the clock case the claim to be rewarded is a number with an agreed budget, and the clock comparisons are themselves independent tests. I would not object if the committee preferred B047 in a later year, and I agree with you that checking the 2018 author contributions should come before any final decision on it. I also agree that the citation for B047 should credit the prediction as much as the experiment.

responses.point: Lindroth asks that the citation state that the concept and first demonstration are Katori's, so that the prize does not read as one for accuracy records, and she disagrees that the 2025 prize makes circuit QED natural.
responses.response: I accept the first point and have changed my citation to name the magic-wavelength concept and its realisation. On circuit QED, I read your argument as pushing me further in the direction I was already moving. I should not argue for B004 as a member who directs WACQT, and your concern that a same-platform follow-up would look like a reward for the hardware race is a fair external view that I cannot make myself. I have therefore dropped B004 from my alternatives and replaced it with B012, which I can assess without that conflict. I disagree only on one nuance: circuit QED is a discovery in its own right, with a clear theory proposal and a first experiment, and a later year, once the credit for the transmon is better understood, would be fine.

responses.point: Kroll argues that the case must stand on the magic-wavelength concept and the 10^-18 demonstration, not on the redefinition of the second, and that Derevianko and Lemonde should not be added.
responses.response: I agree on both. The redefinition is a metrological decision, and I have kept it out of both the citation and my argument. On credit, I am with you on theory: Derevianko's work on magic wavelengths and shifts was important to the budgets, but the prize should go to the demonstration that the condition works and delivers 10^-18. The one place I would add something is your request for a priority check. I support that as a short check in the supporting record before the final ballot, since that is where a dispute could arise, and I do not think the check should change the pair unless the record turns out to be surprising. I also note that, as WACQT management colleagues, we both recuse on B004 if it advances.

responses.point: Pearce, as chair, says that for the clocks he must be able to say what is new beyond better numbers, and that B004 should be held for a later year because of the 2025 prize and the harder attribution.
responses.response: One sentence for the chair: the discovery is that a lattice with a magic wavelength lets large numbers of atoms act as a clock with no first-order trap shift, which brought the systematic uncertainty from the 10^-16 range to 10^-18 and made the clock a probe of redshift and constants. On B004 I agree and I have stepped back from it, for the conflict and the credit reasons you give. I do not share your preference for keeping B017 as the first alternative, only because I do not see a clean split of names for a quantum-simulation prize in this configuration, so my alternatives are B047 and B012. On a two-topic AMO prize, I agree with you that the three-name limit gives no sensible split, so I propose B019 alone.

uncertainties: Whether the committee accepts the magic-wavelength lattice clock as a distinct discovery and not as the next step of a precision-measurement line honoured in 1997, 2005, 2012 and 2018.
The priority record for the first Sr lattice-clock measurements (Katori, JILA, SYRTE) and the status of Lemonde and Derevianko, which I cannot verify from the material I have.
Whether the 2018 twisted bilayer graphene phases and the missing experimental credit (Cao, Fatemi) will be settled by the field in the next few years, which would change my ranking of B047.
Whether the 2016 prize leaves enough room for the Z2 quantum spin Hall effect (B012).
statement.conflict_note: I direct WACQT and work in superconducting circuits. I know the circuit QED groups (Wallraff, Schoelkopf, Blais) and the 2025 laureates, who were guest researchers at Chalmers, so I recuse myself from any discussion of B004 and have removed it from my alternatives. I have no known connection to Katori, Ye, the optical-clock groups, or the candidates in B047 and B012. My own early work on microwave quantum optics is not part of any shortlisted configuration.
